content: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), a condition often triggered by strenuous physical activity, is a common issue that can lead to symptoms such as coughing, shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. This condition can negatively impact physical performance and may even discourage individuals from engaging in physical activity. Management of EIB typically involves preventive strategies, including the use of pharmacological agents before exercise. Among these, mast cell stabilizers, such as nedocromil sodium and sodium cromoglycate, have been shown to reduce the severity of EIB. However, their effectiveness compared to other agents, such as short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs) or anticholinergic agents like atropine or ipratropium bromide, remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to compare the efficacy of a single inhaled dose of mast cell stabilizers to that of SABAs or anticholinergic agents in preventing EIB in individuals aged six years or older with asthma. Additionally, the review aimed to evaluate the effects of combining a mast cell stabilizer with a SABA versus using a SABA alone. The analysis included randomized trials that assessed pulmonary function after exercise, measured as the percentage decrease in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) or peak expiratory flow (PEF) from baseline. Outcomes of interest included complete protection (defined as a maximum post-exercise pulmonary function decline of less than 15%) and clinical protection (defined as a 50% improvement over placebo). The review included 24 trials conducted between 1976 and 1998, involving 518 participants from 13 countries. All the drugs studied were effective in reducing the severity of EIB, though their efficacy varied both between and within individuals. When compared to anticholinergic agents, mast cell stabilizers were found to be more effective. On average, the maximum decline in pulmonary function with mast cell stabilizers was 7.1%, compared to 13.8% with anticholinergic agents (weighted mean difference [WMD] = 6.7%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.3 to 10.0). Mast cell stabilizers also provided a higher proportion of individuals with complete protection (73% vs. 56%; odds ratio [OR] = 2.2; 95% CI: 1.3 to 3.7) and clinical protection (73% vs. 52%; OR = 2.7; 95% CI: 1.1 to 6.4). No significant differences in efficacy were observed based on age, asthma severity, or study quality, and no adverse effects were reported for either drug group. In comparison to SABAs, mast cell stabilizers were less effective at preventing EIB. The average maximum decline in pulmonary function with mast cell stabilizers was 11.2%, compared to 4.3% with SABAs (WMD = 6.8%; 95% CI: 4.5 to 9.2). SABAs provided a greater proportion of individuals with complete protection (85% vs. 66%; OR = 0.3; 95% CI: 0.2 to 0.5) and clinical protection (77% vs. 55%; OR = 0.4; 95% CI: 0.2 to 0.8). There were no significant differences in efficacy based on age, asthma severity, drug type, delivery method, or study quality. Side effects were infrequent, with 11% of participants using SABAs reporting side effects compared to 3% of those using mast cell stabilizers, though this difference was not statistically significant (OR = 0.2; 95% CI: 0.0 to 8.2). The combination of a mast cell stabilizer with a SABA did not provide significant additional benefits in pulmonary function compared to using a SABA alone. The average maximum decline in pulmonary function with the combination was 3.5%, compared to 5.3% with SABAs alone (WMD = 1.8%; 95% CI: -1.1 to 4.6). While the combination therapy provided slightly higher rates of complete protection (80% vs. 68%; OR = 0.5; 95% CI: 0.2 to 1.4) and clinical protection (86% vs. 70%; OR = 0.4; 95% CI: 0.1 to 1.2), these differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.17). No subgroup differences were observed. In conclusion, for individuals with stable asthma, SABAs, mast cell stabilizers, and anticholinergic agents all provide significant protection against EIB with minimal adverse effects. SABAs are generally more effective than mast cell stabilizers, while mast cell stabilizers are more effective than anticholinergic agents. In certain cases, combining a SABA with a mast cell stabilizer may be appropriate. Given the variability in individual responses to these medications, clinicians and patients should collaborate to identify the most effective preventive therapy for each individual.
